newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Top OSCE officials leave before Bosnia local poll.
newsitem.headline: Top OSCE officials leave before Bosnia local poll.

text.p: Several senior Western officials who helped supervise Bosnia's general elections are leaving their posts less than two months before local polls are held, further complicating efforts to organise the November vote, diplomatic sources said on Thursday.

At least five top decision-makers involved in the September 14 national poll have either resigned or decided not to extend their contracts, according to sources in the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
The OSCE, charged with overseeing post-war polls, announced on Wednesday that the director general of elections, Jeff Fischer, had left the organisation because his contract expired.
Sir Kenneth Scott, deputy head of the OSCE mission in Bosnia, has also decided not to renew his contract which expires this month.
Three other international officials, including a legal adviser, an election expert and an official overseeing logistics for the poll have also decided to leave the OSCE mission, officials said.
"Changing the team at this stage is a very poor omen for municipal elections and makes it unlikely they will go smoothly," said Chris Bennett, a spokesman for the International Crisis Group (ICG).
The ICG is a private agency monitoring the peace process.

An OSCE spokesman in Sarajevo, David Foley, denied Fischer was leaving due to a dispute over the timing of the local election, which is scheduled for November 22-24. "There is no dispute and no grudges involved," the spokesman said.
But sources inside the OSCE, who asked not to be named, say some of the officials are leaving in part because they oppose holding the local vote so soon after the general election.
Independent election monitors and analysts say the OSCE will not have enough time before November 22 to solve the problems that plagued national voting.

The municipal poll, which was supposed to coincide with the general election, was postponed by the OSCE due to irregularities with voter registration. Critics say election organisers need months to resolve the problem.

The chief of a team of independent election monitors in Bosnia, Ed van Thijn, said recently the local vote should be held next year to enable organisers to resolve the registration issue and to ensure greater security for refugees crossing ethnic boundary lines to vote.
The U.S. envoy who heads the OSCE mission in Bosnia, Robert Frowick, has pushed for the November date, arguing that the peace process would lose momentum if the vote was delayed.
"Everybody thought the postponement of local elections meant some time in spring, not this soon after the national elections," said an OSCE official who asked not to be named.

"I think we can have local elections in November, but nothing will improve compared to the September 14 elections. The same problems will exist, like voter registration, especially for refugees abroad," said the official, one of those leaving the OSCE.
"It will take several weeks to do that and we simply don't have that time."
One Western relief official in Bosnia said OSCE envoys were worried about being associated with a mission which they believed was rushing ahead with local elections at any cost.
"There is a potential for a disaster in these elections and a lot of people are aware of this and they want out. One can hardly blame them. I wouldn't want to be part of it," said the official.
